lines: Notice the trap built into the question before you even reach for a tool.
Agreeing on a reading and agreeing on who caused what turn out to be two separate problems, and the clocks only ever answer the first one.
So set the clocks aside entirely, and ask what else you actually have to work with.
Before you answer, think about what the log actually has to do with every single pair of events it holds.
It has no option to leave a pair unresolved. Every two events get placed somewhere, whether or not anything connects them.
answer: No, and that gap matters more than it sounds.
A placement the log is forced to make and a fact about which event truly came first are not the same claim.
Two events that never exchanged a message and never shared a process still land somewhere in that log, and that placement is a tie-break, not evidence.

lines: Hold onto exactly what counts here, because the definition is stricter than instinct suggests.
Same service in order counts. A message's send linked to its own receipt counts. A chain built out of those steps counts.
Nothing else does. Outside that chain, in either direction, the relationship has a name too: concurrent.
Watch how little this rule actually needs to know to do its job.
Bump the counter before every event on your own service. Hand that number to anyone you send a message to.
On receipt, jump your own counter past whatever number just arrived. That's the entire mechanism, and it's already enough.
Here's the part worth sitting with, because it looks like it should matter and it doesn't.
Feed this same chain through a simulator that skews the real clocks on purpose, however badly.
The counters never once consult a physical clock, so there is nothing in that skew for them to be fooled by.
Notice what breaking a tie by identity actually buys you here.
It doesn't add any new information about causes. It just guarantees every pair, tied or not, ends up somewhere in one definite line.
That line is exactly strong enough to hand a shared resource to requests in an order nobody can call backwards.
This is the moment to go back and check the promise you were given earlier, because it was narrower than it sounded.
A real cause always gets a smaller number. That direction holds, no exceptions.
But a smaller number proving a real cause was never promised, and two complete strangers can still get numbers that look exactly like one.
Carry forward the exact shape of what you just saw, not a looser version of it.
Happens-before is only program order plus linked sends and receipts, nothing softer than that.
A counter bumped locally, and advanced past every message it receives, respects that chain no matter what any physical clock is doing.
And the line that counter produces is useful precisely because it never goes backwards, even though it still can't tell you who was ever truly independent of whom.
Before you answer, separate what the rule actually guarantees from what would be convenient for it to guarantee.
One direction of that guarantee was proven. Ask yourself whether the other direction ever was.
answer: No, and this is the exact mistake the hook was built to expose.
The guarantee only runs one way: a real cause always gets a larger number afterward.
Two events that never touched each other can still end up with any two numbers at all, and reading that gap as a dependency invents a cause that was never there.
